prompt: On Monday, an engineer sees the Friday launch will likely slip because an API is late. They tell the manager that day instead of waiting.
tells: They tell the manager that day instead of waiting
why: Bad news early gives people options.
trap: No scope trade is proposed yet; the move is the early warning.

prompt: A project's status was 'green' every week, then 'red' the day before launch. The director asks why no one flagged the trouble sooner.
tells: why no one flagged the trouble sooner
why: Surprises at the deadline mean risk was hidden.
trap: Cutting scope might help now; the failure was not warning early.

prompt: A senior notices the plan depends on another team that has no time this quarter, and raises it in week one's planning review.
tells: raises it in week one's planning review
why: Name risks as soon as you see them.
trap: It isn't unclear requirements; it's a threat to delivery.

prompt: Halfway through a two-week task, an engineer finds it's really four weeks of work. They post an update with the new estimate and why.
tells: They post an update with the new estimate and why
why: Share new information about dates as soon as you have it.
trap: The estimate was wrong, but the act is warning about the date.

prompt: In a behavioral interview, a candidate describes telling a client three weeks ahead that a feature was at risk, with two options to choose from.
tells: three weeks ahead that a feature was at risk
why: Early warning with options builds trust.
trap: Options are offered, but the story's point is warning early.

prompt: Before launch, an engineer spots that a compliance review hasn't been booked and could take a month. She flags it to the program manager right away.
tells: could take a month. She flags it to the program manager right away
why: A hidden schedule risk needs flagging now.
